items.prompt: Why do many flowers produce sweet nectar deep inside them, where a visitor has to push past the pollen to reach it?

options.label: Nectar is a waste product the flower needs to get rid of
options.feedback: Nectar is built specifically from sugar the plant spends effort making. A waste product would not be worth manufacturing at a cost.

options.label: Nectar keeps the flower's tissues from drying out
options.feedback: Nectar sits in the open, exposed to air, which makes it a poor way to hold moisture in. Its sweetness serves a visitor, not the flower's own water balance.

options.label: Nectar is a reward that lures a visitor into brushing against the flower's pollen on the way to it
options.feedback: Reaching the nectar forces a visitor's body past the pollen-bearing and pollen-receiving parts, picking pollen up or leaving it behind without meaning to.

options.label: Nectar dissolves the flower's own pollen so it can be released
options.feedback: Pollen is released by the anther drying and splitting open, a process nectar has no part in — the two sit in different places on the flower.

items.ok_title: A reward with a hidden cost
items.ok_line: The visitor pays for its meal without ever knowing it.
items.ko_line: Ask what an animal does with its body while it is busy reaching a reward placed just past the flower's pollen.
items.exp_title: A prize placed behind the pollen
items.exp_text: Nectar has no purpose for the flower itself; it exists purely to be found and eaten by something else. Placing it deep inside, past the anthers and the stigma, means a visitor reaching for it cannot avoid brushing against those parts on the way in and out. The flower gets its pollen carried for free, hidden inside what looks like a simple meal.

items.prompt: Why are wind-pollinated flowers, like those on grasses, usually small, dull-coloured and without any scent?

options.label: They have nothing to attract, so building colour or scent would be wasted effort
options.feedback: Wind carries pollen without needing to be lured anywhere, so spending resources on bright petals or perfume would buy nothing.

options.label: Wind destroys any bright colour before it can be seen
options.feedback: Colour is a stable pigment in the petal tissue. Moving air has no effect on it at all.

options.label: These flowers bloom only at night, when colour cannot be seen anyway
options.feedback: Many wind-pollinated grasses flower in broad daylight. Their plainness has nothing to do with when they open.

options.label: They save their colour for the seeds instead
options.feedback: A seed's colouring, when it has any, serves a different purpose again, such as camouflage. It is not colour saved up from an earlier stage.

items.ok_line: Attraction only pays for itself if something needs attracting.
items.ko_line: Ask what colour and scent are actually for, and whether a wind-pollinated flower has any use for that at all.
items.exp_text: Colour and scent exist only to be noticed by an animal that can then be lured toward the pollen. A flower pollinated by wind has no such visitor to impress, since the air will carry its pollen regardless of how the flower looks or smells. Instead it spends its resources on producing huge amounts of loose, light pollen that the wind can catch and scatter.

items.prompt: Some flowers carry patterns that are invisible to a human eye but stand out clearly to a bee. What are these patterns for?

options.label: They mark which flowers have already wilted
options.feedback: A wilted flower usually changes shape and droops, a signal any visitor can already see without needing a hidden pattern.

options.label: They warn a visitor that the nectar has run out
options.feedback: A depleted flower more often changes its overall colour so it can be recognised at a glance, rather than hiding a warning in a pattern only some visitors can see.

options.label: They help the flower absorb extra sunlight for growth
options.feedback: A petal's pigments do many jobs, but gathering light for the plant's own growth belongs to the leaves, not to markings meant to be seen by a visitor.

options.label: They act as guide lines pointing a visitor straight toward the nectar and the pollen
options.feedback: A bee's eyes can pick up light beyond what a human sees, and the flower uses that to paint lines the bee can follow inward, straight past the pollen.

items.ok_line: The lines are drawn for an eye that can actually read them.
items.ko_line: Some visitors can see a colour range humans cannot. What would a flower gain from painting something only they can see?
items.exp_title: Runway lines only a bee can read
items.exp_text: A bee's eyes are sensitive to a band of light beyond what a human eye can detect, and some flowers use that extra range to paint patterns invisible to us. Those patterns run like lines toward the centre of the flower, guiding an arriving bee straight to the nectar rather than leaving it to search at random. The shortest route to the reward also happens to be the route that brushes it past the flower's pollen.

items.prompt: Why do some flowers open only at dusk or during the night, rather than in daylight?

options.label: Darkness protects their petals from being damaged by heat
options.feedback: Many night-opening flowers grow in mild climates with no daytime heat strong enough to damage a petal. Timing is not being set to avoid it.

options.label: They are timed to be open when the pollinators they depend on are active
options.feedback: A flower visited mainly by night-flying visitors gains nothing by being open and offering nectar during the day, when almost none of its visitors are around to use it.

options.label: Sunlight would bleach their scent away
options.feedback: Scent comes from compounds released steadily from the petals, not stored dye that light could fade. It would keep releasing scent in daylight just as well.

options.label: Closing during the day keeps rainwater out of the flower
options.feedback: Rain falls at all hours regardless of season or time of day, so timing based on rainfall would not line up with a strict day-versus-night pattern.

items.ok_line: There is no reward in being open when nobody is looking for it.
items.ko_line: Producing nectar and scent costs the plant something. What determines whether that cost is worth paying at a given hour?
items.exp_title: A schedule matched to a visitor
items.exp_text: Keeping nectar and scent on offer costs a flower resources whether or not anything comes to collect them. A flower that depends on visitors active mainly after dark gains nothing by staying open through the day, when few of those visitors are around, so it opens instead in the evening or at night to match their schedule. The flower's own timing is built around when the pollinator it needs will actually be flying.

items.prompt: Some flowers, such as lantana, change colour soon after they have been pollinated. What is that colour change doing?

options.label: It signals to visitors that this flower no longer needs a visit, sending them toward flowers that still do
options.feedback: A visitor learns to avoid the changed colour and heads instead for the flowers still offering nectar, so pollen is not wasted on a flower already done.

options.label: It signals that the flower has run out of water
options.feedback: The colour switch happens on well-watered plants right after pollination succeeds, tied to that event rather than to thirst.

options.label: It warns visitors that the plant has become poisonous
options.feedback: The plant's chemistry has not changed at this point; only the flower's pigment has. Nothing about it has become newly dangerous.

options.label: It is a side effect of the petals starting to dry out
options.feedback: The colour shift happens while the petals are still soft and fresh, well before any drying begins.

items.ok_line: The flower is redirecting traffic, not simply fading.
items.ko_line: The timing lines up with a very specific event. What does the flower gain by advertising that event to a passing visitor?
items.exp_text: Once a flower has been pollinated it no longer benefits from another visit, but a plant usually has many flowers open at once, some done and some not. Changing colour right after pollination gives a visitor an easy signal to avoid the finished flowers and head for ones still offering nectar. The plant's pollen and the visitor's time are both spent more efficiently because of that one small change.

items.prompt: Certain orchids briefly trap a visiting insect inside a chamber in the flower before letting it go. What does that delay achieve?

options.label: It gives the flower time to make more nectar for the visitor
options.feedback: Nectar production runs on its own pace and does not speed up because a visitor happens to be held inside for a moment.

options.label: It stops the visitor from stealing pollen without paying for it
options.feedback: The visitor is not being punished or charged. It is simply being kept in place long enough for a specific step to happen.

options.label: It keeps the visitor in place long enough for pollen to be properly attached to its body before it can leave
options.feedback: The forced path out past the flower's pollen-bearing parts ensures the visitor is dusted correctly, instead of leaving too soon and missing them.

options.label: It lets the flower check whether the visitor is carrying the right kind of pollen
options.feedback: A flower has no way to sense or check what a visitor is carrying. The trap only controls where the visitor's body goes on its way out.

items.ok_line: The delay is not a punishment. It is a forced, useful detour.
items.ko_line: The visitor is released, unharmed, after a short time. What could a brief, forced delay be used to guarantee?
items.exp_text: A visitor that flies straight in and straight back out might never touch the flower's pollen-bearing parts at all. By briefly holding the visitor inside a chamber, the flower forces it along a single narrow exit route that passes directly against the anthers or the stigma. The pause is not about time passing — it is about making sure the exit path cannot be skipped.

items.prompt: Why does a single flower often make far more pollen grains than the number of ovules it actually needs to fertilize?

options.label: Extra pollen is stored as food for the developing seeds
options.feedback: A seed is fed by the ovule's own tissue and later by the plant's sugars, not by leftover pollen grains sitting nearby.

options.label: Carrying pollen on wind or on an animal's body wastes most of it before it ever reaches another flower
options.feedback: A pollen grain can be dropped, brushed off, eaten, or simply land somewhere useless, so only a small fraction of what is released ever finds its way to a matching stigma.

options.label: Each ovule actually needs several pollen grains to be fertilized
options.feedback: A single ovule needs only one successful pollen grain reaching it. The surplus is not being spent on any one ovule needing more.

options.label: Older pollen grains stop working, so new ones must keep replacing them
options.feedback: A flower typically releases its pollen over a short, active window rather than continuously replacing spoiled batches — the surplus is about loss in transit, not spoilage.

items.ok_line: Most of what is sent out is never going to arrive.
items.ko_line: Think about the trip a single pollen grain has to survive between one flower and another.
items.exp_text: A pollen grain released into the wind or brushed onto an animal has to survive being carried, avoid landing somewhere useless, and still arrive on the matching part of another flower of the right kind. Nearly all of it fails at some point along that path. Producing far more pollen than the ovules strictly require is how a flower compensates for how much of it never completes the journey.

items.prompt: Why do many flowers rely on both bright colour and scent together, rather than just one or the other?

options.label: Colour and scent are simply two names for the same signal
options.feedback: A visitor detects colour with its eyes and scent with entirely separate organs, so the two are picked up through different senses, not one signal under two names.

options.label: Scent exists only to disguise the smell of the flower's own pollen
options.feedback: Pollen itself has little scent of its own to cover up, so masking it cannot be what the flower's fragrance is for.

options.label: Colour is used only to repel the wrong kind of visitor
options.feedback: Bright colour in most flowers works the opposite way, drawing visitors closer rather than warning them off. Repelling is not what it is doing here.

options.label: Colour guides a visitor from a distance, while scent can still guide it up close or in poor light
options.feedback: A visitor can spot bright colour from far away, but scent keeps working at close range or after dark, when colour becomes harder to see.

items.ok_line: One works from far off, the other keeps working once the visitor is close.
items.ko_line: Colour and scent are picked up by different senses and carry over different distances. What does having both let a flower cover?
items.exp_title: A long-range signal and a close-range one
items.exp_text: Bright colour stands out against green leaves from a distance, drawing a visitor's attention before it is anywhere near the flower. Scent works differently: it still carries once the visitor is close, in shade, or flying after dark when colour is hard to make out. Combining both means the flower can be found from far away and still be located once colour alone is no longer enough.

items.prompt: Why can some flowers be pollinated by only one particular kind of visitor, such as a flower with a very long, narrow tube matched to a long-tongued moth?

options.label: The tube's shape and depth match that visitor's mouthparts, so only it can reach the nectar and pick up pollen correctly
options.feedback: Any visitor without a matching length simply cannot reach the nectar at the bottom, so it never gets close enough to the flower's pollen either.

options.label: The flower produces a scent that only that one kind of visitor can detect
options.feedback: Many different visitors can sense a flower's scent from a distance. What actually excludes most of them here is being unable to reach the nectar once they arrive.

options.label: The flower's colour is invisible to every other kind of visitor
options.feedback: Colour differences between visitors' eyes are a matter of degree, not an on-off switch, and cannot alone explain why every other visitor is shut out completely.

options.label: Other visitors are frightened away by the tube's narrow opening
options.feedback: A narrow tube does not threaten a visitor; it simply fails to fit their mouthparts, so they are excluded by shape rather than by fear.

items.ok_title: A lock and its one key
items.ok_line: The nectar is only ever out of reach for the wrong length of tongue.
items.ko_line: The nectar sits at a fixed depth. What decides whether a visitor's mouthparts can actually get down to it?
items.exp_title: A depth only one visitor can reach
items.exp_text: A flower with an unusually long, narrow tube keeps its nectar at a depth most visitors' mouthparts simply cannot reach. A visitor whose tongue matches that depth can push all the way down to feed, and in doing so presses its head or body against the flower's pollen-bearing parts on the way. Every other visitor is excluded not by choice but by shape, unable to reach the reward at all.

items.prompt: Why do flowers so often arrange their pollen-producing stamens and pollen-receiving stigma so a visitor's body cannot avoid brushing both?

options.label: It keeps the pollen from blowing away in the wind
options.feedback: Pollen is held on the anther by its own sticky or textured surface, not by the position of the stigma nearby. Wind loss is not what this arrangement is preventing.

options.label: It protects the stigma from being damaged by the visitor
options.feedback: Placing the stigma directly in a visitor's path exposes it to contact rather than shielding it, which is the opposite of protection.

options.label: It forces a visitor's body to pick up pollen and later deposit it on another flower's stigma in the same spot
options.feedback: Positioning both parts along the visitor's one entry route means the same patch of its body that collects pollen here will brush against a stigma on the next flower it visits.

options.label: It lets the flower absorb any pollen the visitor happens to be carrying, no matter where it came from
options.feedback: A stigma is chemically matched to accept pollen only from the same kind of flower, and its position controls contact, not absorption from just anywhere.

items.ok_line: The route in is built so nothing important can be skipped.
items.ko_line: A visitor follows roughly the same path into every flower of a given kind. What does placing both parts along that path guarantee happens twice?
items.exp_title: Positioned along the one route in
items.exp_text: A visitor reaching for nectar tends to follow the same path into every flower of a given kind, brushing against whatever sits along that path on the way. Placing the pollen-bearing stamens and the pollen-receiving stigma directly along that route means the same part of the visitor's body picks up pollen here and can deposit it on the very next matching flower it visits. Nothing about the visitor's behaviour needs to change — only where the flower's own parts happen to sit.
